findings.source_quote: ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει
findings.english_quote: For the one who does not wish to listen has understood
findings.issue: The contextual subject-reading is intelligible, especially after the preceding sentence, but the note presents it without explaining the irregular supplied construction: ὁ precedes the finite θέλει, not a participle. A materially different object-reading would result from interpreting the printed ὁ as an orthographically irregular neuter relative, conventionally ὃ: he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear. The existing note discusses ἔγνω but does not disclose this syntactic and orthographic uncertainty.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note identifying the supplied ὁ and distinguishing any proposed normalization to ὃ from the printed reading. Preserve the alternative “For he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear.” If retaining the current subject-reading, explain its contextual basis and its treatment of the irregular construction. The verified print need not be rechecked merely because its syntax is unusual; the revised rendering and disclosure require fresh review.

findings.english_quote: The printed οὕπω has a rough breathing and circumflex-like spelling where the negative adverb meaning “not yet” is conventionally written οὔπω. The context unambiguously requires the negative sense.
findings.issue: The source note inaccurately characterizes the accent. The supplied οὕπω has rough breathing and an acute, not a circumflex. The relevant difference from conventional οὔπω is the breathing. The main rendering’s negation is faithful; this is a minor error in the source disclosure, not an unresolved reading or missing meaning.
findings.suggested_revision: Replace the note with: “The supplied print reads οὕπω, with rough breathing and an acute; the negative adverb is conventionally written οὔπω, with smooth breathing and an acute. The English renders the contextual negative sense ‘not yet.’ οὔπω is a proposed orthographic normalization, not the supplied reading.” Treat this as a disclosed orthographic feature, without requesting renewed print verification.

findings.source_quote: τὸ εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν παραδοθὲν ὑμῖν τιμᾶν ὄνομα
findings.english_quote: the name entrusted to you for honoring his sole rule
findings.issue: The rendering shifts the object of honoring from the entrusted name to God’s sole rule. The infinitive τιμᾶν belongs to the construction concerning the name entrusted to the recipients to honor; εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν supplies its relation or purpose, not a straightforward direct object equivalent to “his sole rule.” This obscures the source’s explicit contrast between honoring the name and subjecting that same name to insult. The lexical note repeats rather than resolves this shift.
findings.suggested_revision: Use a source-transparent construction such as “the name entrusted to you to honor with regard to his sole rule.” Revise the note to preserve the name as the object of τιμᾶν and explain that εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν may qualify the entrusting or the honoring. Submit the replacement for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς τέως παρειληφότες ὑβρίσατε ὃ ἐδόθη ὑμῖν, ἵνα ὡς ἂν αὐτῷ χρήσῃσθε, εἰς τὸ ὄντως αὐτοῦ ὄνομα λογισθῇ
findings.english_quote: Rather, you received for the present what was given to you and insulted it, so that whatever use you made of it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name
findings.issue: The restructuring moves “what was given to you” into the receiving clause and leaves the purpose clause immediately dependent on “insulted it.” It consequently suggests that the audience insulted the designation for the purpose of having its use reckoned against the true name. In the Greek, ἵνα immediately follows ὃ ἐδόθη ὑμῖν and can explain why the designation was given. That attachment fits the designation’s representative function. Attachment to ὑβρίσατε remains a syntactic alternative, but neither the alternative nor the reason for the draft’s apparent choice is disclosed; the existing note addresses only the implicit subject of λογισθῇ.
findings.suggested_revision: Keep παρειληφότες subordinate and retain the giving clause beside its purpose: “Rather, having received it for the present, you insulted what was given to you in order that whatever use you made of it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name.” Explain in a note that the purpose is understood as belonging to ἐδόθη because the received designation represents the actual name, while attachment to ὑβρίσατε is syntactically possible. Review the revised wording afresh, including whether its English attachment is sufficiently clear.
